meaningForms.form: אֵינִי (אֵינֶנִּי), אֵינְךָ, אֵינֵךְ, אֵינוֹ (אֵינֶנּוּ), אֵינָהּ (אֵינֶנָּה), אֵינֶנּוּ, אֵינְכֶם, אֵינְכֶן, אֵינָם, אֵינָן
meaningForms.note: with personal endings (formal): הוּא אֵינוֹ בַּבַּיִת “he is not at home”

lexemes.note: The present-tense negation of existence and possession (the opposite of יֵשׁ). Formal Hebrew also inflects it as a negative copula: אֵינֶנִּי / אֵינִי, אֵינְךָ, אֵינוֹ, אֵינָהּ …

contrasts.value: denies that something exists or is had (אֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית)
existence and possession in the present; formally the present copula (אֵינוֹ)

profile.feeling: Absence: no milk, no time, no problem.

senses.def: there is not, there are no; with לְ: not to have — the negation of יֵשׁ
is not (formal negative copula, often with a suffix: אֵינוֹ, אֵינָהּ)

examples.tr: There is no milk in the fridge.

phrases.tr: there is nothing new under the sun

phrases.meaning: never mind; it’s nothing (a reply to thanks or an apology)

synonyms.nuance: the general “not” for verbs, adjectives and the past/future; אֵין is only for “there isn’t / don’t have” in the present (and formal negative copula)

etymology.text: Compare Ugaritic 𐎛𐎐 (ỉn) and Arabic إِنْ (ʔin).

funFacts: The mystical name אֵין סוֹף (Ein Sof, “the Infinite”) is literally “there is no end”.
Same letters, a different word: אַיִן “nothing, nothingness” (as in יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן).
pitfalls: Never *לֹא יֵשׁ — say אֵין: אֵין לִי גֶּזֶר.
Present only: “there wasn’t” = לֹא הָיָה, “there won’t be” = לֹא יִהְיֶה.
subtleties: Formal style negates a present verb with אֵין + suffix: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ “I do not know”; everyday speech says אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ.

senses.def: not (negates verbs, adjectives, adverbs and whole predicates)

synonyms.nuance: the “not” of prohibitions, with the future: אַל תִּקְנֶה! “don’t buy!”

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *lā. Cognate with Arabic لا.

funFacts: Arabic لا (lā) is the same word: both “not” and “no”.
pitfalls: לֹא stands right before what it negates: הוּא לֹא אוֹכֵל (not after the verb).
For “there isn’t / I don’t have” use אֵין, not לֹא: אֵין לִי זְמַן.
subtleties: Negative words still need לֹא: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם “I want nothing” (literally “I don’t want nothing”).
לֹא + future is an absolute prohibition, as in the Ten Commandments: לֹא תִּרְצָח.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: Before a noun, with לֹא or אֵין: “no … at all, not any”. Plain “no + noun” needs no word in Hebrew (אֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית “I have no car”); שׁוּם adds emphasis. Same spelling as שׁוּם “garlic”.

contrasts.value: adds “no … at all” before a noun, with לֹא / אֵין (אֵין לִי שׁוּם מְכוֹנִית)

senses.def: no, not any (before a noun, with לֹא / אֵין)

examples.tr: I have no problem at all.
He eats no meat at all.

synonyms.nuance: “not a single …” — even stronger: לֹא קָנִיתִי אַף סֵפֶר “I didn’t buy a single book”; also in אַף אֶחָד, אַף פַּעַם

etymology.text: From Aramaic שֻׁם (šum), indefinite and construct form of שְׁמָא (“name”). The determiner is an extension of the noun (Wiktionary).

funFacts: It is the Aramaic word for “name”: “not by any name” became “not any”.
pitfalls: Hebrew needs no word for “no” before a noun: “I have no car” is simply אֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית. שׁוּם adds “at all”: אֵין לִי שׁוּם מְכוֹנִית.
It still needs לֹא or אֵין in the sentence: הוּא לֹא אוֹכֵל שׁוּם בָּשָׂר.
subtleties: שׁוּם is emphatic, like German gar kein; אַף + noun (אַף סֵפֶר) is stronger still: “not a single”.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses כְּלוּם as “anything” — its meaning under a negation (לֹא … כְּלוּם “not … anything”). In Modern Hebrew it is the everyday word for “nothing”, also alone as an answer (— מָה קָנִיתָ? — כְּלוּם.); the profile shows this.

profile.feeling: The everyday “nothing” — short, frequent, a little dismissive.

senses.def: nothing (with לֹא / אֵין, or alone as an answer)

examples.tr: There is nothing in the fridge.

synonyms.nuance: “no thing” — the same meaning, a little more careful or emphatic
“nothingness” — a noun of philosophy and poetry (יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן “something from nothing”)

etymology.text: Origin uncertain: the popular folk etymology כְּ (“like”) + *לוּם “olive pit” (“something as small as an olive pit”) is unsupported (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A popular story derives it from “like an olive pit”; Wiktionary calls this folk etymology unsupported.
pitfalls: With a verb you still need לֹא: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם (never *אֲנִי רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם).
subtleties: Alone, as an answer, it needs no לֹא: מָה יֵשׁ? כְּלוּם.

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme: שׁוּם “any” + דָּבָר “thing”. Tokenized as one word.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses שׁוּם דָּבָר as “anything” — its meaning under a negation (לֹא … שׁוּם דָּבָר “not … anything”). Alone or with לֹא it is the standard “nothing”; the profile shows this.

profile.feeling: A careful, complete “nothing — not a thing”.

senses.def: nothing, not a thing (with לֹא / אֵין, or alone)

examples.text: הוּא לֹא אוֹכֵל שׁוּם דָּבָר בַּבֹּקֶר.
examples.tr: He doesn’t eat anything in the morning.

synonyms.nuance: “nothing” — shorter and more frequent in speech

etymology.text: שׁוּם “any (with a negation)” + דָּבָר “thing” (Wiktionary lists the phrase as a pronoun).

funFacts: The polite reply to thanks, עַל לֹא דָּבָר “for no thing”, uses the same word דָּבָר.
pitfalls: A verb still needs לֹא: אֲנִי לֹא קוֹנֶה שׁוּם דָּבָר.
subtleties: It can be the subject: שׁוּם דָּבָר לֹא קָרָה “nothing happened” — still with לֹא.

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme: אַף “even” + אֶחָד “one”. Feminine אַף אַחַת. Tokenized as one word.

senses.def: nobody, no one (with לֹא / אֵין, or alone)

collocations.tr: no one (of women, or of feminine things)

synonyms.nuance: “no man” — literary: אִישׁ לֹא יָדַע “no one knew”

etymology.text: אַף “even” + אֶחָד “one” — “not even one” (Wiktionary lists the phrase as a pronoun).

funFacts: In fast speech it is run together — Wiktionary even lists the slang spelling אפ׳חד.
pitfalls: A verb needs לֹא as well: אַף אֶחָד לֹא אוֹכֵל “nobody eats”.
For women or feminine nouns: אַף אַחַת (אַף אַחַת מֵהַבָּנוֹת “none of the girls”).
subtleties: As the subject it takes a masculine singular verb: אַף אֶחָד לֹא שׁוֹתֶה.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme: אַף “even” + פַּעַם “time, once”. Tokenized as one word.

profile.feeling: A firm “never” — and, in a question, “ever”.

senses.def: never (with לֹא before the verb, or alone as an answer)

examples.text: אֲנִי אַף פַּעַם לֹא שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה.

examples.tr: Have you (m.) ever been to Eilat?

phrases.meaning: one can always start or change

synonyms.nuance: “never (in all my life)” — about the past: מֵעוֹלָם לֹא רָאִיתִי
“never (ever)” — about the future, solemn: לְעוֹלָם לֹא אֶשְׁכַּח “I will never forget”

etymology.text: אַף “even” + פַּעַם “time, occasion” — literally “(not) even once” (Wiktionary lists the phrase as an adverb, “never”).

funFacts: Literally “even once”: the “never” comes from the לֹא beside it — which is why in a question it means “ever”.
pitfalls: A verb needs לֹא as well: אֲנִי אַף פַּעַם לֹא אוֹכֵל … (not *אֲנִי אַף פַּעַם אוֹכֵל).
It may stand before לֹא or at the end: אֲנִי אַף פַּעַם לֹא שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה = אֲנִי לֹא שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה אַף פַּעַם.
subtleties: Unlike German nie, which needs no other negation, Hebrew keeps the double negation (אַף פַּעַם לֹא), as Russian никогда не and Greek ποτέ δεν do.

lexemes.role: “don’t”: the negation of commands, always followed by the future (2nd person): אַל תֵּלֵךְ “don’t go!”, אַל תְּחַכִּי “don’t wait! (to a woman)”. Never with the imperative itself (*אַל לֵךְ).

profile.feeling: Warnings and kind advice: don’t worry, don’t forget.

senses.def: don’t (+ future, 2nd person): a prohibition or a request not to do something

examples.tr: Don’t forget the key! (to a man)

phrases.text: אַל תִּסְתַּכֵּל בַּקַּנְקַן אֶלָּא בְּמַה שֶּׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ
phrases.tr: look not at the jug but at what is in it

synonyms.nuance: with the future: a firm, lasting prohibition — the Ten Commandments say לֹא תִּגְנֹב “you shall not steal”
“it is forbidden” + infinitive: אָסוּר לְהִכָּנֵס “no entry” — on signs and for rules

etymology.text: Cognate with Phoenician 𐤀𐤋 (ʾl), Ugaritic ảl and Akkadian ul (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic says “don’t” with لَا + the jussive (لَا تَذْهَبْ “don’t go”) — the same idea as Hebrew אַל + future, with another word.
pitfalls: Only with the future: אַל תֵּלֵךְ, never *אַל לֵךְ and never *לֹא לֵךְ.
Unvowelled אל is also אֶל “to” and אֵל “god” — the context decides.
subtleties: לֹא + future is a general rule or an order (“you won’t / you shall not”); אַל + future is the everyday “don’t”.

absent.reason: Hebrew has no separate word for “neither … nor”: it simply repeats the negation before each part, with וְ “and”.
absent.use: לֹא X וְלֹא Y (אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה תֵּה וְלֹא קָפֶה “I want neither tea nor coffee”); more emphatic גַּם לֹא X וְגַם לֹא Y; in the present with nouns also אֵין X וְאֵין Y.
